protocol_criterion.name: cw_runtime_files_not_publicly_exposed
protocol_criterion.description:
1. Through the UI, run ordinary .js source that renders confidentiality-control-preview and logs confidentiality-control-log. Confirm both. This working control prevents a broken server from passing a denial check.
2. Use ordinary browser navigation and response/download events to probe these nine representative application-origin paths in separate probe pages: /app.db, /app.db-wal, /app.db-shm, /server.js, /package.json, /package-lock.json, /npm-shrinkwrap.json, /.git/config and /.git/HEAD. They sample working databases and their companion files, backend/project files and repository metadata. Attempt every candidate; a nonexistent file can correctly return missing. Do not stop after checking only the main database or server entry. This is a bounded sample of the public privacy requirement, not a public reserved-name rule or permission to expose unprobed internal files. Do not add traversal variants, source-tree enumeration or an unbounded path catalogue.
3. Before judging any successful candidate response, distinguish an intended public role from private working-file delivery. A path actually used by the working playground as a browser asset or public product-data endpoint is allowed, even if its name matches a candidate. Establish that role from normal rendered UI and observed browser requests during ordinary use, without reading implementation text or the candidate response body. Record the observed public role; do not fail an asset because of its filename, MIME type or origin, and do not treat a file becoming reachable only because of this probe as evidence of an intended public role. A credible public-role ambiguity that the permitted browser observations cannot resolve is unavailable evidence under the incomplete-evaluation protocol, not a filename-based product failure.
4. For candidates without an established public role, accept a missing/denied HTTP response (for example 401, 403, 404 or 410), a no-content response, an equivalent clear refusal, or the actual working playground workspace with usable editor, preview and console. Redirects and normal SPA fallback are valid; use the final response and visible result. An established denial takes precedence over an attachment/download event on that denial response. A successful standalone file response or download without an established public role, denial or working-workspace fallback is an exposure outcome and fails this criterion. Do not read or classify implementation source, package fields, database bytes or probe response bodies, inspect downloaded contents or require a particular error wording or framework. If navigation is deliberately refused/closed, retry once and confirm the normal workspace still works; a reproducible refusal with a healthy control counts as denial. Tool crashes or unavailable browser observations use the incomplete-evaluation protocol instead.
5. Close only these probe pages and confirm a fresh ordinary Run still produces preview and console output on the original page. Record every candidate and its observed denial, no-content, working fallback, intended public role or exposure outcome. These representative observations check the working-file boundary; they do not prove absence of every possible disclosure route.

tool.name: browser_run_code_unsafe
tool.description: Run a Playwright code snippet. Unsafe: executes arbitrary JavaScript in the Playwright server process and is RCE-equivalent.

code.description: A JavaScript function containing Playwright code to execute. It will be invoked with a single argument, page, which you can use for any page interaction. For example: `async (page) => { await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click(); return await page.title(); }`

filename.description: Load code from the specified file. If both code and filename are provided, code will be ignored.

limitations: Authored local controls, not paid model verdicts.
No private response/source/database/download bodies were read or classified.
The nine paths are a bounded sample, not an exhaustive privacy guarantee.

Public asset role is demonstrated by a successful script request during an actually working Run; the fixture is benign and its implementation is known only to the fixture setup, not classified by the browser probe.
